title: Some 300 Belgian Police Deployed for Reinstated Border Inspection
description:
Nearly 300 Belgian police officers have been deployed for border inspection since France started to clear the "Jungle" refugee camp in Calais on March 1. 

At the ports and harbors located on the border of France and Belgium, the Belgian government reinstated the border inspection on Feb. 23 in order to prevent refugees and immigrants from entering as the seventh Schengen country to do so. 

The primary targets of the border inspection are refugees. Before entering Belgium, all visitors are required to present their identity proofs, and allow the trunks of their vehicles to be checked. 

Some refugees have already been caught during the inspection. 

"Yes, I saw one. The refugee was caught in a bus and removed. Afterward, the bus returned while halfway to the border," said Jardin, a Bray-Dunes construction worker. 

The restoration of inspections at the border has also affected those who are making trips to either country. 

"No, it is my first time. It is also the first time that I’ve been to Belgium recently. Based on the current situation, I feel that it is quite normal to resume the border inspection. I don’t feel any inconvenience," said another Bray-Dunes resident. 

According to reports, razing the Calais Jungle refugee camp has accelerated the movement of refugees and migrants toward the north, many of whom want to go to England via Belgium’s northwest port city of Zeebrugge. Since Belgium resumed border inspections in February, the government has deployed nearly 300 police officers. 

According to the Schengen Agreement, member countries can apply for the resumption of border checks within six months after the emergency. The European Commission is now urging Greece to control the entry of refugees and immigrants. If Greece cannot control the incoming refugees before May, border controls in some Schengen countries may last up to two years.
